title: NoSQL Data Models
summary: Key-value, document, column-family, and graph models — picked by access pattern, not by hype.

slides.markdown:
"NoSQL" isn't one data model — it's four distinct ones, each shaped for a different access pattern: key-value, document, column-family, and graph. Picking the wrong one because it's popular, rather than because it fits your queries, is one of the most common system-design mistakes.

This topic walks through all four with the query each is built for, so "what data store would you use here" becomes a pattern-matching question instead of a guess.

slides.sectionTitle: Key-value stores: the simplest model and its ceiling
slides.markdown:
A **key-value store** (Redis, DynamoDB in its simplest mode, Memcached) maps one opaque key to one opaque value — the database doesn't know or care what's inside the value. Lookups by key are extremely fast and trivially partitionable, because the key alone decides which node owns the data.

The ceiling is exactly that opacity: you can't query by anything other than the key. Want "all users signed up this week"? The store can't help — you'd need a secondary index or a separate system. Key-value shines for session storage, caching, and any lookup that's always "give me the value for this ID."

slides.sectionTitle: Document stores: nested data and flexible schema
slides.markdown:
A **document store** (MongoDB, Couchbase) stores each record as a semi-structured document — usually JSON — that can nest arrays and objects inside it, and different documents in the same collection can have different fields. That maps naturally to how application code already thinks about an object: a user document can embed their addresses and preferences instead of joining three tables to reassemble them.

Queries can filter and index on fields inside the document, which is more flexible than pure key-value, but still weaker than SQL for relationships that span documents — modeling a many-to-many relationship (users and the groups they belong to) usually means denormalizing IDs into both sides rather than a join.

slides.sectionTitle: Column-family stores: wide rows for write-heavy, time-series-like data
slides.markdown:
A **column-family store** (Cassandra, HBase, Bigtable) organizes data as rows identified by a key, where each row can have a different, large set of columns grouped into families — and columns for a row are stored together on disk, sorted by column name. This layout is built for very high write throughput: appending a new column (like a new sensor reading, timestamped) is a cheap, sequential write, not an update to a fixed-width row.

It's the natural fit for write-heavy, append-mostly data — event logs, metrics, time-series-like feeds — where you almost always query "give me this row's data in this time range" rather than joining across rows.

slides.sectionTitle: Graph databases: when relationships are the query
slides.markdown:
A **graph database** (Neo4j, Amazon Neptune) stores entities as nodes and relationships as first-class edges with their own properties, and is built to traverse those edges fast — "friends of friends who also follow this page" is a cheap graph traversal but an expensive multi-join query in a relational database, and an awkward fit for key-value or document models entirely.

The signal to reach for a graph database is when the *relationships themselves* are what you're querying — recommendation engines, fraud-ring detection, social graphs — not just when your data happens to have some foreign keys.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the same data modeled four ways
slides.markdown:
![The same user, orders, and products dataset drawn four ways: key-value blob, nested document, wide-column with appended columns, and a graph of User/Order/Product nodes](assets/four-data-models.svg)

The same facts — a user, their orders, the products in those orders — get shaped completely differently depending on which model stores them. A key-value store flattens it to one blob per lookup key; a document store keeps the nesting; a column-family store spreads it across appended columns; a graph makes the relationships themselves queryable.

There's no "most correct" shape here — each shape is optimized for a different question you'll ask of the same data.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: choosing a model by access pattern, not by hype
slides.markdown:
| Model | Best for | Weak at |
|---|---|---|
| Key-value | Lookup by ID, caching, sessions | Any query that isn't "by key" |
| Document | Nested, object-shaped data with per-record variation | Relationships spanning many documents |
| Column-family | Very high write volume, time-ordered append data | Ad-hoc queries on non-key columns |
| Graph | Traversing relationships (friends-of-friends, fraud rings) | Simple lookups, high write volume |

**How to decide:** write down your top two or three actual queries first — "get user by ID," "get all of a user's orders," "find paths between these two accounts" — then pick the model that makes those queries cheap, not the model that's trending.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: modeling a document store like a relational schema
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll just make a `users` collection and an `orders` collection and reference IDs between them, like foreign keys."

**Why it's wrong:** document stores don't do server-side joins efficiently — that pattern forces the application to fetch a user, then fetch each referenced order in a separate round trip, which is slower than a single relational join and pushes the join logic (and its bugs) into every place that reads the data.

**Correct model:** embed data that's read together and rarely needs independent updates (an order's line items live inside the order document), and only reference across documents for data that's genuinely separate, large, or shared across many parents (a `userId` on an order, not the whole user embedded).

slides.sectionTitle: The wide-partition trap: a column-family key that grows without bound
slides.markdown:
A column-family store's row key decides which node (and which physical partition) owns that row's data — so a naive design keying time-series data by a coarse identifier, say `sensor_id` alone with every reading appended as a new column, means one popular sensor's row grows forever and all its data lives on one partition indefinitely. A sensor reporting every second for a year accumulates over 31 million columns under a single key, on a single node, no matter how many nodes the cluster has.

This is a **hot partition**, and it doesn't show up in early testing — it appears months later as one node in the cluster consistently running hotter (higher CPU, higher latency) than its siblings, exactly proportional to how unevenly "popular" different keys turn out to be in production traffic.

The standard fix is **bucketing the key**: instead of `sensor_id` alone, key by `sensor_id + date_bucket` (e.g. one row per sensor per day), so the same sensor's data spreads across many rows, and therefore potentially many partitions, over time, bounding how large any single row can grow regardless of how long the sensor keeps reporting.
